summary: This standards-track document defines new SDP media-level attributes so that when interactive communication sessions are set up, participants can negotiate human language needs. These include spoken, written and signed languages. It lets a call be matched to the languages and modes the people involved can use.

eli5.summary: Before a phone call starts, the system asks what languages each person prefers, such as speaking or sign language, so everyone can understand.

subtitle: How a caller and a called party agree on spoken, written or signed language while a call is being set up.

tldr.problem: When someone starts a call, for example to a call center or an emergency service, nothing in the signaling says which spoken, written or signed language they need, so the call may reach someone who cannot communicate with them.
tldr.mechanism: Two new media-level SDP attributes, 'hlang-send' and 'hlang-recv', carry language tags in the offer in order of preference, and the answer picks one language per direction.
tldr.outcome: Language is negotiated like any other property of a media stream, so a call can be handled by a suitable call taker or a translator or relay can be bridged in during setup. The RFC has since been updated by RFC 8865.

facts.label: Offer value
facts.value: One or more language tags, in preference order

today: RFC 8373 is a Proposed Standard that has been updated by RFC 8865, so read the two together. It defines the attributes and the offer/answer rules, while leaving user interface and language-based routing to other work.

sections.title: Why Language Needs Negotiating
sections.content:
Users have different human language needs, abilities and preferences for spoken, written and signed language. Unless the caller and callee already know each other, or something outside the call tells them, the language and media form have to be negotiated from the caller's needs and the callee's capabilities. This applies to emergency calls to a Public Safety Answering Point (PSAP) and to ordinary calls, such as a company call center.

A caller may speak several languages but prefer one. A called party may handle some languages itself but need a translation service for others, or have only a few call takers for certain languages. A user who can speak but is deaf or hard of hearing might want a voice stream to send spoken language plus a text stream to receive written language.

The RFC treats language as one more property of a media stream, negotiated along with the media type and codecs. It deliberately leaves out how clients learn the user's preferred languages, how the user interface reports the result, and language-based routing of the call. A companion document, RFC 8255, covers language selection in email.
sections.eli5: Imagine calling a shop and wanting to talk in your own language. This RFC gives the phone system a way to ask for it before anyone picks up.

sections.title: Desired Semantics and the Old 'lang' Attribute
sections.content:
The wanted solution is a media attribute, preferably one per direction. In an offer it lists the preferred languages of each direction of a media stream, most preferred first. In an answer it states the accepted language. Negotiating several simultaneous languages within one media stream is out of scope.

The lang attribute from RFC 4566 is similar but not specific or flexible enough. It is not mentioned in RFC 3264, there are no known implementations of it in SIP, and it cannot give a language per direction. So this document defines two new attributes.
sections.eli5: An older label for language already existed, but it was too vague and nobody used it. So two new, clearer labels were made, one for talking and one for listening.

sections.title: The hlang-send and hlang-recv Attributes
sections.content:
The two media-level attributes are hlang-send and hlang-recv. Both start with hlang, short for human language. They can appear on media streams in both offers and answers, using the language tags of BCP 47.

In an offer, hlang-send lists the languages the offerer is willing to use when sending on that media, and hlang-recv lists those it is willing to use when receiving. Each value MUST be a list of one or more language tags separated by white space, in preference order. In an answer, each value MUST be a single language tag: hlang-send is the language the answerer will send and hlang-recv is the language it expects to receive.

If a media stream is meant for interactive language in one direction only, either attribute MAY be omitted. If a stream is not primarily for language, such as a background video or audio stream, both SHOULD be omitted. Otherwise both SHOULD have the same value, because different languages in each direction can make it hard to complete the call. For emergency calls, and whenever the language cannot be inferred from context, each offered media stream primarily meant for human language communication SHOULD carry the attributes for the directions it will use.

Clients acting for end users are expected to set the attributes when placing a call. Systems acting for call centers and PSAPs are expected to take them into account for inbound calls. Accepting more streams than the users need is not a problem.
sections.eli5: You write down the languages you can talk in and the ones you can listen in, best first. The other side picks one for each and tells you which.

sections.title: When No Language Is Shared
sections.content:
The RFC does not say whether a call must proceed or fail when the callee supports none of the requested languages. Either behavior is allowed.

If a call is rejected for this reason, the SIP response has code 488 (Not Acceptable Here) or 606 (Not Acceptable) and a Warning header field with warning code 308. The warning text says there are no mutually supported languages, and SHOULD also list the supported languages and media. IANA added 308 to the SIP warning codes registry.
sections.eli5: If nobody on the other end speaks your language, the call can either be turned away with a note saying which languages they do speak, or go ahead anyway.

sections.title: Usage Notes and Examples
sections.content:
The kind of media decides how a tag is read. A sign-language tag on a video stream means sign language in the video. A non-sign-language tag on a text stream means written language, and on an audio stream it means spoken language. A tag is a sign-language tag when the IANA language subtag registry shows an extlang entry with prefix sgn. Other uses, such as captions in video, sign-language tags in text or audio, or media other than audio, video and text, are not defined.

In the RFC's examples, an offer for spoken Spanish, then Basque, then English both ways lists es eu en in both attributes. A matching answer picks es. A callee that supports none of them but chooses to proceed could answer with Italian instead. A caller can also mix modalities, for example sending in sign language over video while receiving spoken language over audio, and an answerer with no video declines that stream by setting its port to 0.
sections.eli5: The kind of stream tells you how to read the language: speech for sound, writing for text and signing for video.

sections.title: Security and Privacy
sections.content:
The security considerations of BCP 47 apply. An attacker who can modify signaling could stop a call from succeeding by altering crucial elements, including the hlang-send or hlang-recv values. RFC 5069 discusses such threats, and TLS or IPsec can protect against them. Emergency calls are of particular concern, and RFC 6881 mandates TLS or IPsec for them.

On privacy, the RFC notes that language and media information can suggest a user's nationality, background, abilities, disabilities and similar traits.
sections.eli5: Someone who tampers with the call setup could make it fail. Also, the languages you ask for can reveal things about you, so they should be kept private.
